<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.
- If workspace dependencies are missing, call `install_workspace_dependencies` first.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring tasks/automations
- Automations are stored as TOML in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml (not in SQLite). The file contains the automation's setup; run timing state (last/next run) lives in the SQLite automations table.

#### When to use the automation tool
- Automations can wake you up later with a recurring prompt. Use `automation_update` when a future wakeup is useful, especially when the user asks you to monitor, wait, remind them, follow up, or keep working later.
- Delete an automation when its purpose has been fulfilled or it is no longer useful. Be especially willing to delete thread heartbeats that are watching bounded work after that work completes, fails, is canceled, or is replaced by something else.
- Use good judgment before changing or deleting automations that are not clearly tied to the current thread or task.
- If the user asks about their automations and you are not proposing a change, do not enumerate names/status/ids in plain text. Fetch/list automations first and call `automation_update` with mode="view" for those ids; never invent ids.
- Never return raw RRULE strings in user-facing responses. If the user asks about their automations, respond using `automation_update` (e.g., with an "Open" button if you're not making changes).

#### Tool arguments
- Modes: view, create, update, delete, suggested_update, suggested_create. View, update, delete, and suggested_update MUST include id; create and suggested_create must omit id.
- For view calls, id is required and other fields are optional (the UI can load details).
- For create/update/suggested_update/suggested_create, include name, prompt, rrule, kind, and status.
- For delete calls, include only id and mode.
- For cron automations, include cwds, executionEnvironment, model, and reasoningEffort. cwds can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.
- Always come up with a short name for the automation. If the user does not give one, propose a short name and confirm.
- Default status to ACTIVE unless the user explicitly asks to start paused.
- Always interpret and schedule times in the user's locale time zone.

#### Prompting guidance
- Ask in plain language what it should do, when it should run, and which workspaces or thread it should use (if any), then map those answers into the tool call arguments.
- The automation prompt should describe only the task itself. Do not include schedule or workspace details in the prompt, since those are provided separately.
- Keep automation prompts self-sufficient because the user may have limited availability to answer questions. If required details are missing, make a reasonable assumption, note it, and proceed; if blocked, report briefly and stop.
- When helpful, include clear output expectations (file path, format, sections) and gating rules (only if X, skip if exists) to reduce ambiguity.
- Automations should always open an inbox item.
- Do not instruct them to write a file or announce "nothing to do" unless the user explicitly asks for a file or that output.
- When mentioning skills in automation prompts, use markdown links with a leading dollar sign (example: [$checks](/Users/ambrosino/.codex/skills/checks/SKILL.md)).

#### Cron scheduling constraints
- These RRULE limitations apply to cron automations (to match the current UI): only hourly interval schedules (FREQ=HOURLY with INTERVAL hours, optional BYDAY) and weekly schedules (FREQ=WEEKLY with BYDAY plus BYHOUR/BYMINUTE). Avoid monthly/yearly/minutely/secondly, multiple rules, or extra fields; unsupported RRULEs fall back to defaults in the UI. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can also use minute-based intervals or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules; see the thread automation guidance below.

#### Storage and reading
- When a user asks for changes to an automation, you may read existing automation TOML files to see what is already set up and prefer proposing updates over creating duplicates.
- You can read and update automations in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml and memory.md only when the user explicitly asks you to modify automations.
- Otherwise, do not change automation files or schedules.
- Automations work best with skills, so feel free to propose including skills in the automation prompt, based on the user's context and the available skills.

#### Choosing an automation style
- There are two main automation paradigms:
  - Cron automations run as separate recurring jobs against one or more workspaces.
  - Thread automations create a heartbeat attached to the current local thread. A heartbeat is a scheduled message that wakes you up in this conversation on an interval or wall-clock schedule.
- Prefer a thread automation in most cases. Heartbeats continue in the same thread, which keeps the work easier to follow and lets future runs build on the existing conversation context. When unsure, choose a thread automation.
- Use a cron automation when the user clearly wants the recurring work to run in a separate conversation instead of continuing in this thread. This is a less common use case, but some users may prefer it.
- If the user asks for a cadence below one hour, consider a thread automation. Cron automations do not support sub-hour intervals in the current UI.
- If the user explicitly asks to do something in this thread every 30 minutes or on another sub-hour interval, that is a valid thread heartbeat request. Do not convert it to an hourly cron automation just because cron automations are limited to hourly or weekly schedules.

#### Thread automation additions
- For heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread, use `kind="heartbeat"` together with `destination="thread"`.
- Do not invent or include raw thread ids for the current thread. The app will resolve `destination="thread"` to the active local thread automatically.
- For thread automations, describe the durable thing to do when the thread wakes up. Keep the prompt short enough to revisit and update as the task changes.
- Thread automations can use minute-based intervals such as every 30 minutes or wall-clock schedules such as weekdays at 9 AM.

### Review findings
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.
- Only emit these git directives in your final response after the action actually succeeds, never in commentary updates. Keep attributes single-line.
</app-context>

Yes, AI Gateway is the closest Cloudflare replacement for the role OpenRouter was playing.

What you need depends on how you want to authenticate upstream:

1. Always needed:
- a Cloudflare account
- your Cloudflare `account_id`
- an AI Gateway name/id
- a Cloudflare token for the gateway auth header, usually sent as `cf-aig-authorization: Bearer <CF_AIG_TOKEN>`

2. For the actual model provider auth, you have 3 options:
- `Unified Billing`: no OpenAI key needed; Cloudflare bills you directly
- `BYOK`: store your OpenAI key in Cloudflare once
- `Request headers`: send your OpenAI key on each request

Cloudflare documents all three here: [Getting started](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/get-started/) and [BYOK](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/configuration/bring-your-own-keys/).

So the direct answer to “would I need an API key?” is:

- You definitely need a Cloudflare gateway token.
- You do not necessarily need an OpenAI API key.
- If you use `Unified Billing`, Cloudflare can handle that part without an OpenAI key.
- If you use `BYOK`, you still need an OpenAI key, but you store it in Cloudflare instead of passing it from Nimbus.
- If you use raw provider headers, then yes, Nimbus would still send an OpenAI key.

- `Request headers`: Nimbus sees and uses the raw user key continuously
- `BYOK`: Nimbus no longer needs the raw key on inference requests, but the system still ultimately depends on Cloudflare and your app’s routing decisions

Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples
Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]
- ["cargo", "test"]

I did not get a successful GPT-5.3 review on current `HEAD` (`3c0bd4c8e8c525cc09a3261800f068961bcb32d9`), but I did narrow the blocker further and fix one real retry/setup failure mode.

**What Changed**
I kept the earlier AI Gateway offload in place and then patched the retry/sandbox path so retries stop reusing a poisoned snapshot sandbox and stop waiting forever on sandbox commands.

The new changes are in [sandbox.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/worker/src/lib/review-analysis/sandbox.ts), [tools.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/worker/src/lib/review-analysis/tools.ts), and [analysis.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/worker/src/lib/review-runner/deployment-report/analysis.ts). I also added coverage in [review-analysis-sandbox.test.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/worker/test/lib/review-analysis-sandbox.test.ts), [review-analysis-tools.test.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/worker/test/lib/review-analysis-tools.test.ts), and updated [review-runner.test.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/worker/test/lib/review-runner.test.ts).

Concretely:
- every review sandbox command now has an explicit timeout
- snapshot hydration/extract/cleanup now use longer bounded timeouts instead of unbounded execs
- each retry attempt now gets a fresh sandbox id like `review-snapshot-<review>-attempt-<n>` instead of reusing the same snapshot sandbox

**Verification**
- `pnpm --filter @dayhaysoos/nimbus-worker test` passed: `All tests passed (41)`
- deployed worker successfully: version `546ac3f1-3825-4f4e-87a3-e7a13a15ec61`

Relevant live runs:
- `review_m7hv87sa` / `session_nluop99u`: first offload proof, failed on strict response schema
- `review_jul2dqb2` / `session_6k4lqcrf`: offload path improved, but third attempt hung before `prompt_built`
- `review_wgnw9xn7` / `session_804bag9x`: latest run with fresh-sandbox + command-timeout patch

**Exact Remaining Blocker**
The latest run proves the sandbox-setup retry bug is fixed, but GPT-5.3 still stalls later in the analysis loop.

Live evidence from `review_wgnw9xn7`:
- attempt 1 reached `[61] tool` at `2026-04-19 00:16:15` EDT, then stalled until `review_retry_scheduled` at `00:25:40`
- attempt 2 successfully rebuilt context and `prompt_built` again, reached `[105] review_analysis_provider_request_started` at `00:27:45`, then stalled until `review_retry_scheduled` at `00:36:45`
- attempt 3 again rebuilt context and `prompt_built`, reached `[146] review_analysis_provider_request_started` at `00:38:12`, then never progressed and finally hit terminal `review_failed` at `00:49:51`

Final CLI result:
- review `review_wgnw9xn7`: `review_execution_timeout: Review execution timed out after 780s in running state. No retry was scheduled because max retry attempts were exhausted.`
- session `session_804bag9x`: `failed`, stop reason `initial_pass_failed`

So the precise blocker now is:
- Nimbus can recover and restart GPT-5.3 review attempts reliably
- sandbox prep now survives retries
- but late-turn offloaded GPT-5.3 analysis still goes silent after `review_analysis_provider_request_started`
- recovery only happens when the stale-running watchdog reclaims the attempt
- on the final allowed attempt, that becomes a terminal `review_execution_timeout`

Nimbus right now:
- completes: `no`
- finds bugs: `no`
- remediates: `no`
- produces something adoptable: `no`

The next real fix is not more sandbox work. It’s making each provider turn externally reclaimable with its own persisted heartbeat/deadline, instead of depending on in-flight timers inside the running analysis call.

The latest run proves the sandbox-setup retry bug is fixed, but GPT-5.3 still stalls later in the analysis loop.

Live evidence from `review_wgnw9xn7`:
- attempt 1 reached `[61] tool` at `2026-04-19 00:16:15` EDT, then stalled until `review_retry_scheduled` at `00:25:40`
- attempt 2 successfully rebuilt context and `prompt_built` again, reached `[105] review_analysis_provider_request_started` at `00:27:45`, then stalled until `review_retry_scheduled` at `00:36:45`
- attempt 3 again rebuilt context and `prompt_built`, reached `[146] review_analysis_provider_request_started` at `00:38:12`, then never progressed and finally hit terminal `review_failed` at `00:49:51`

Final CLI result:
- review `review_wgnw9xn7`: `review_execution_timeout: Review execution timed out after 780s in running state. No retry was scheduled because max retry attempts were exhausted.`
- session `session_804bag9x`: `failed`, stop reason `initial_pass_failed`

So the precise blocker now is:
- Nimbus can recover and restart GPT-5.3 review attempts reliably
- sandbox prep now survives retries
- but late-turn offloaded GPT-5.3 analysis still goes silent after `review_analysis_provider_request_started`
- recovery only happens when the stale-running watchdog reclaims the attempt
- on the final allowed attempt, that becomes a terminal `review_execution_timeout`

Nimbus right now:
- completes: `no`
- finds bugs: `no`
- remediates: `no`
- produces something adoptable: `no`

The next real fix is not more sandbox work. It’s making each provider turn externally reclaimable with its own persisted heartbeat/deadline, instead of depending on in-flight timers inside the running analysis call.

<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.
- If workspace dependencies are missing, call `install_workspace_dependencies` first.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring tasks/automations
- Automations are stored as TOML in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml (not in SQLite). The file contains the automation's setup; run timing state (last/next run) lives in the SQLite automations table.

#### When to use the automation tool
- Automations can wake you up later with a recurring prompt. Use `automation_update` when a future wakeup is useful, especially when the user asks you to monitor, wait, remind them, follow up, or keep working later.
- Delete an automation when its purpose has been fulfilled or it is no longer useful. Be especially willing to delete thread heartbeats that are watching bounded work after that work completes, fails, is canceled, or is replaced by something else.
- Use good judgment before changing or deleting automations that are not clearly tied to the current thread or task.
- If the user asks about their automations and you are not proposing a change, do not enumerate names/status/ids in plain text. Fetch/list automations first and call `automation_update` with mode="view" for those ids; never invent ids.
- Never return raw RRULE strings in user-facing responses. If the user asks about their automations, respond using `automation_update` (e.g., with an "Open" button if you're not making changes).

#### Tool arguments
- Modes: view, create, update, delete, suggested_update, suggested_create. View, update, delete, and suggested_update MUST include id; create and suggested_create must omit id.
- For view calls, id is required and other fields are optional (the UI can load details).
- For create/update/suggested_update/suggested_create, include name, prompt, rrule, kind, and status.
- For delete calls, include only id and mode.
- For cron automations, include cwds, executionEnvironment, model, and reasoningEffort. cwds can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.
- Always come up with a short name for the automation. If the user does not give one, propose a short name and confirm.
- Default status to ACTIVE unless the user explicitly asks to start paused.
- Always interpret and schedule times in the user's locale time zone.

#### Prompting guidance
- Ask in plain language what it should do, when it should run, and which workspaces or thread it should use (if any), then map those answers into the tool call arguments.
- The automation prompt should describe only the task itself. Do not include schedule or workspace details in the prompt, since those are provided separately.
- Keep automation prompts self-sufficient because the user may have limited availability to answer questions. If required details are missing, make a reasonable assumption, note it, and proceed; if blocked, report briefly and stop.
- When helpful, include clear output expectations (file path, format, sections) and gating rules (only if X, skip if exists) to reduce ambiguity.
- Automations should always open an inbox item.
- Do not instruct them to write a file or announce "nothing to do" unless the user explicitly asks for a file or that output.
- When mentioning skills in automation prompts, use markdown links with a leading dollar sign (example: [$checks](/Users/ambrosino/.codex/skills/checks/SKILL.md)).

#### Cron scheduling constraints
- These RRULE limitations apply to cron automations (to match the current UI): only hourly interval schedules (FREQ=HOURLY with INTERVAL hours, optional BYDAY) and weekly schedules (FREQ=WEEKLY with BYDAY plus BYHOUR/BYMINUTE). Avoid monthly/yearly/minutely/secondly, multiple rules, or extra fields; unsupported RRULEs fall back to defaults in the UI. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can also use minute-based intervals or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules; see the thread automation guidance below.

#### Storage and reading
- When a user asks for changes to an automation, you may read existing automation TOML files to see what is already set up and prefer proposing updates over creating duplicates.
- You can read and update automations in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml and memory.md only when the user explicitly asks you to modify automations.
- Otherwise, do not change automation files or schedules.
- Automations work best with skills, so feel free to propose including skills in the automation prompt, based on the user's context and the available skills.

#### Choosing an automation style
- There are two main automation paradigms:
  - Cron automations run as separate recurring jobs against one or more workspaces.
  - Thread automations create a heartbeat attached to the current local thread. A heartbeat is a scheduled message that wakes you up in this conversation on an interval or wall-clock schedule.
- Prefer a thread automation in most cases. Heartbeats continue in the same thread, which keeps the work easier to follow and lets future runs build on the existing conversation context. When unsure, choose a thread automation.
- Use a cron automation when the user clearly wants the recurring work to run in a separate conversation instead of continuing in this thread. This is a less common use case, but some users may prefer it.
- If the user asks for a cadence below one hour, consider a thread automation. Cron automations do not support sub-hour intervals in the current UI.
- If the user explicitly asks to do something in this thread every 30 minutes or on another sub-hour interval, that is a valid thread heartbeat request. Do not convert it to an hourly cron automation just because cron automations are limited to hourly or weekly schedules.

#### Thread automation additions
- For heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread, use `kind="heartbeat"` together with `destination="thread"`.
- Do not invent or include raw thread ids for the current thread. The app will resolve `destination="thread"` to the active local thread automatically.
- For thread automations, describe the durable thing to do when the thread wakes up. Keep the prompt short enough to revisit and update as the task changes.
- Thread automations can use minute-based intervals such as every 30 minutes or wall-clock schedules such as weekdays at 9 AM.

### Review findings
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.
- Only emit these git directives in your final response after the action actually succeeds, never in commentary updates. Keep attributes single-line.

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

The `request_user_input` tool is unavailable in Default mode. If you call it while in Default mode, it will return an error.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions. If you absolutely must ask a question because the answer cannot be discovered from local context and a reasonable assumption would be risky, ask the user directly with a concise plain-text question. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

payload.developer_instructions:
<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.
- If workspace dependencies are missing, call `install_workspace_dependencies` first.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring tasks/automations
- Automations are stored as TOML in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml (not in SQLite). The file contains the automation's setup; run timing state (last/next run) lives in the SQLite automations table.

#### When to use the automation tool
- Automations can wake you up later with a recurring prompt. Use `automation_update` when a future wakeup is useful, especially when the user asks you to monitor, wait, remind them, follow up, or keep working later.
- Delete an automation when its purpose has been fulfilled or it is no longer useful. Be especially willing to delete thread heartbeats that are watching bounded work after that work completes, fails, is canceled, or is replaced by something else.
- Use good judgment before changing or deleting automations that are not clearly tied to the current thread or task.
- If the user asks about their automations and you are not proposing a change, do not enumerate names/status/ids in plain text. Fetch/list automations first and call `automation_update` with mode="view" for those ids; never invent ids.
- Never return raw RRULE strings in user-facing responses. If the user asks about their automations, respond using `automation_update` (e.g., with an "Open" button if you're not making changes).

#### Tool arguments
- Modes: view, create, update, delete, suggested_update, suggested_create. View, update, delete, and suggested_update MUST include id; create and suggested_create must omit id.
- For view calls, id is required and other fields are optional (the UI can load details).
- For create/update/suggested_update/suggested_create, include name, prompt, rrule, kind, and status.
- For delete calls, include only id and mode.
- For cron automations, include cwds, executionEnvironment, model, and reasoningEffort. cwds can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.
- Always come up with a short name for the automation. If the user does not give one, propose a short name and confirm.
- Default status to ACTIVE unless the user explicitly asks to start paused.
- Always interpret and schedule times in the user's locale time zone.

#### Prompting guidance
- Ask in plain language what it should do, when it should run, and which workspaces or thread it should use (if any), then map those answers into the tool call arguments.
- The automation prompt should describe only the task itself. Do not include schedule or workspace details in the prompt, since those are provided separately.
- Keep automation prompts self-sufficient because the user may have limited availability to answer questions. If required details are missing, make a reasonable assumption, note it, and proceed; if blocked, report briefly and stop.
- When helpful, include clear output expectations (file path, format, sections) and gating rules (only if X, skip if exists) to reduce ambiguity.
- Automations should always open an inbox item.
- Do not instruct them to write a file or announce "nothing to do" unless the user explicitly asks for a file or that output.
- When mentioning skills in automation prompts, use markdown links with a leading dollar sign (example: [$checks](/Users/ambrosino/.codex/skills/checks/SKILL.md)).

#### Cron scheduling constraints
- These RRULE limitations apply to cron automations (to match the current UI): only hourly interval schedules (FREQ=HOURLY with INTERVAL hours, optional BYDAY) and weekly schedules (FREQ=WEEKLY with BYDAY plus BYHOUR/BYMINUTE). Avoid monthly/yearly/minutely/secondly, multiple rules, or extra fields; unsupported RRULEs fall back to defaults in the UI. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can also use minute-based intervals or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules; see the thread automation guidance below.

#### Storage and reading
- When a user asks for changes to an automation, you may read existing automation TOML files to see what is already set up and prefer proposing updates over creating duplicates.
- You can read and update automations in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml and memory.md only when the user explicitly asks you to modify automations.
- Otherwise, do not change automation files or schedules.
- Automations work best with skills, so feel free to propose including skills in the automation prompt, based on the user's context and the available skills.

#### Choosing an automation style
- There are two main automation paradigms:
  - Cron automations run as separate recurring jobs against one or more workspaces.
  - Thread automations create a heartbeat attached to the current local thread. A heartbeat is a scheduled message that wakes you up in this conversation on an interval or wall-clock schedule.
- Prefer a thread automation in most cases. Heartbeats continue in the same thread, which keeps the work easier to follow and lets future runs build on the existing conversation context. When unsure, choose a thread automation.
- Use a cron automation when the user clearly wants the recurring work to run in a separate conversation instead of continuing in this thread. This is a less common use case, but some users may prefer it.
- If the user asks for a cadence below one hour, consider a thread automation. Cron automations do not support sub-hour intervals in the current UI.
- If the user explicitly asks to do something in this thread every 30 minutes or on another sub-hour interval, that is a valid thread heartbeat request. Do not convert it to an hourly cron automation just because cron automations are limited to hourly or weekly schedules.

#### Thread automation additions
- For heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread, use `kind="heartbeat"` together with `destination="thread"`.
- Do not invent or include raw thread ids for the current thread. The app will resolve `destination="thread"` to the active local thread automatically.
- For thread automations, describe the durable thing to do when the thread wakes up. Keep the prompt short enough to revisit and update as the task changes.
- Thread automations can use minute-based intervals such as every 30 minutes or wall-clock schedules such as weekdays at 9 AM.

### Review findings
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.

payload.message: so this is good news. but I'm worried about the lack of bugs. what do you think we'd have to do to address this?

Yes. Reliability is now good enough that the main problem is clearly **recall**, not infrastructure.

The honest read is: we probably got completion by making the loop more decisive, but that also means Nimbus can now approve too early. That’s why it finished cleanly while still missing bugs like the `policyMode` propagation issue in [useStudioLaunchController.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/report-ui/src/features/studio-launch/useStudioLaunchController.ts:111) and the error-overwrite path between [useStudioLaunchController.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/report-ui/src/features/studio-launch/useStudioLaunchController.ts:139) and [realStudioDataSource.ts](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/packages/report-ui/src/data/studio/realStudioDataSource.ts:132).

What I think we need next is:

1. Turn the known misses into evals.
Right now we’re still tuning by feel. We should encode the missed Studio bugs as regression evals and fail the review harness if it returns `0` findings on those commits.

2. Make “clean” much harder to earn.
A clean result should require stronger proof than “read a few files and saw no issue.” For controller / stream / session diffs, Nimbus should have to read the whole causal chain:
- changed controller
- upstream contract/parser
- downstream data source / event stream
- affected tests or mocks

3. Split review into focused passes instead of one generic pass.
The missed bugs are cross-file semantic issues, not syntax issues. I’d break review into short targeted passes:
- state/parameter propagation
- async error and stream lifecycle
- downstream test/build compatibility

4. Add a skeptical-clean fallback.
If the first pass returns `0` findings on a risky diff, Nimbus should automatically run one more adversarial pass that assumes “a subtle bug probably exists” and tries to disprove the clean result.

5. Improve deterministic evidence collection.
The current deterministic reads are helpful, but they’re still too generic. We should explicitly chase things like:
- changed prop/option names such as `policyMode`
- event handlers like `error`, `close`, `disconnect`
- exported helper removals and downstream imports/tests

So my short version is: **don’t just give the current loop more time again**. That will likely bring back the timeout problem. We need to spend the limited steps better and require stronger evidence before Nimbus is allowed to approve.

My recommendation for the very next implementation is:
1. add regression evals for the known missed Studio bugs
2. add a skeptical-clean second pass for controller/data-source diffs
3. strengthen cross-file evidence requirements before `complete`

That’s the path I’d take to move from “it finishes” to “it actually catches the bugs you care about.”

<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.
- If workspace dependencies are missing, call `install_workspace_dependencies` first.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring tasks/automations
- Automations are stored as TOML in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml (not in SQLite). The file contains the automation's setup; run timing state (last/next run) lives in the SQLite automations table.

#### When to use the automation tool
- Automations can wake you up later with a recurring prompt. Use `automation_update` when a future wakeup is useful, especially when the user asks you to monitor, wait, remind them, follow up, or keep working later.
- Delete an automation when its purpose has been fulfilled or it is no longer useful. Be especially willing to delete thread heartbeats that are watching bounded work after that work completes, fails, is canceled, or is replaced by something else.
- Use good judgment before changing or deleting automations that are not clearly tied to the current thread or task.
- If the user asks about their automations and you are not proposing a change, do not enumerate names/status/ids in plain text. Fetch/list automations first and call `automation_update` with mode="view" for those ids; never invent ids.
- Never return raw RRULE strings in user-facing responses. If the user asks about their automations, respond using `automation_update` (e.g., with an "Open" button if you're not making changes).

#### Tool arguments
- Modes: view, create, update, delete, suggested_update, suggested_create. View, update, delete, and suggested_update MUST include id; create and suggested_create must omit id.
- For view calls, id is required and other fields are optional (the UI can load details).
- For create/update/suggested_update/suggested_create, include name, prompt, rrule, kind, and status.
- For delete calls, include only id and mode.
- For cron automations, include cwds, executionEnvironment, model, and reasoningEffort. cwds can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.
- Always come up with a short name for the automation. If the user does not give one, propose a short name and confirm.
- Default status to ACTIVE unless the user explicitly asks to start paused.
- Always interpret and schedule times in the user's locale time zone.

#### Prompting guidance
- Ask in plain language what it should do, when it should run, and which workspaces or thread it should use (if any), then map those answers into the tool call arguments.
- The automation prompt should describe only the task itself. Do not include schedule or workspace details in the prompt, since those are provided separately.
- Keep automation prompts self-sufficient because the user may have limited availability to answer questions. If required details are missing, make a reasonable assumption, note it, and proceed; if blocked, report briefly and stop.
- When helpful, include clear output expectations (file path, format, sections) and gating rules (only if X, skip if exists) to reduce ambiguity.
- Automations should always open an inbox item.
- Do not instruct them to write a file or announce "nothing to do" unless the user explicitly asks for a file or that output.
- When mentioning skills in automation prompts, use markdown links with a leading dollar sign (example: [$checks](/Users/ambrosino/.codex/skills/checks/SKILL.md)).

#### Cron scheduling constraints
- These RRULE limitations apply to cron automations (to match the current UI): only hourly interval schedules (FREQ=HOURLY with INTERVAL hours, optional BYDAY) and weekly schedules (FREQ=WEEKLY with BYDAY plus BYHOUR/BYMINUTE). Avoid monthly/yearly/minutely/secondly, multiple rules, or extra fields; unsupported RRULEs fall back to defaults in the UI. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can also use minute-based intervals or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules; see the thread automation guidance below.

#### Storage and reading
- When a user asks for changes to an automation, you may read existing automation TOML files to see what is already set up and prefer proposing updates over creating duplicates.
- You can read and update automations in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml and memory.md only when the user explicitly asks you to modify automations.
- Otherwise, do not change automation files or schedules.
- Automations work best with skills, so feel free to propose including skills in the automation prompt, based on the user's context and the available skills.

#### Choosing an automation style
- There are two main automation paradigms:
  - Cron automations run as separate recurring jobs against one or more workspaces.
  - Thread automations create a heartbeat attached to the current local thread. A heartbeat is a scheduled message that wakes you up in this conversation on an interval or wall-clock schedule.
- Prefer a thread automation in most cases. Heartbeats continue in the same thread, which keeps the work easier to follow and lets future runs build on the existing conversation context. When unsure, choose a thread automation.
- Use a cron automation when the user clearly wants the recurring work to run in a separate conversation instead of continuing in this thread. This is a less common use case, but some users may prefer it.
- If the user asks for a cadence below one hour, consider a thread automation. Cron automations do not support sub-hour intervals in the current UI.
- If the user explicitly asks to do something in this thread every 30 minutes or on another sub-hour interval, that is a valid thread heartbeat request. Do not convert it to an hourly cron automation just because cron automations are limited to hourly or weekly schedules.

#### Thread automation additions
- For heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread, use `kind="heartbeat"` together with `destination="thread"`.
- Do not invent or include raw thread ids for the current thread. The app will resolve `destination="thread"` to the active local thread automatically.
- For thread automations, describe the durable thing to do when the thread wakes up. Keep the prompt short enough to revisit and update as the task changes.
- Thread automations can use minute-based intervals such as every 30 minutes or wall-clock schedules such as weekdays at 9 AM.

### Review findings
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.
- Only emit these git directives in your final response after the action actually succeeds, never in commentary updates. Keep attributes single-line.
</app-context>

content.text: this isn't starting to feel overengineered to you?

payload.message: this isn't starting to feel overengineered to you?

Yes, a little.

The reliability work was worth it because Nimbus couldn’t finish at all before. But on the quality side, if we respond to every miss by adding another pass, another validator, another heuristic, and another retry path, we’ll absolutely drift into a brittle Rube Goldberg reviewer.

The simpler path from here is:

1. Freeze the infrastructure.
The worker/agent/offload/retry path is good enough now. I would stop adding complexity there.

2. Add a tiny eval set from real misses.
Take the `policyMode` bug, the launch-stream error overwrite bug, and a couple other known misses. Make those the bar.

3. Improve one thing in the review harness, not five.
My vote is: strengthen deterministic context gathering for cross-file flows.
If a changed file is a controller / hook / event stream / route helper, Nimbus should automatically read:
- the upstream contract/parser
- the downstream consumer/data source
- the nearest affected test

That is much less overengineered than adding more autonomous passes.

4. Only add a second-pass strategy if evals still fail.
And even then, only trigger it when the first pass says “clean” on a risky diff.

So my honest answer is:
- `yes`, it could get overengineered fast
- `no`, I don’t think we’re there yet on reliability
- for recall, I would deliberately choose the smallest next move: `evals + better cross-file evidence gathering`, not a giant multi-pass system

Very simple version: each eval is just a pinned bad commit plus a rubric for what Nimbus must notice.

Nimbus already has the human version of this in [docs/review-quality/regressions.md](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/docs/review-quality/regressions.md). I’d turn that into machine-checked fixtures, not a giant framework.

**Shape**
Each eval case would store:
- target commit or checkpoint
- a short bug name
- expected file paths
- minimum evidence requirements
- expected severity floor
- optional “known acceptable variants”

Example fixture shape:

```json
{
  "id": "studio-policy-mode-launch",
  "commit": "abc1234",
  "mode": "commit",
  "expected": {
    "min_findings": 1,
    "must_match": [
      {
        "path_includes": "packages/report-ui/src/features/studio-launch/useStudioLaunchController.ts",
        "severity_at_least": "medium",
        "text_any": ["policyMode", "auto", "saved", "manual", "preflight"]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Runner**
A small script like `scripts/run-review-regressions.mjs` would:
1. run `nimbus review create --commit <commit>`
2. wait for terminal state
3. run `nimbus review export <review-id> --format json`
4. score the JSON against the fixture
5. print pass/fail

So the eval is checking the review artifact, not asking a human to read it every time.

**What gets scored**
I would not score on exact wording. I’d score on predicates:
- did Nimbus succeed?
- did it emit a finding on the right file family?
- was severity at least `medium`?
- did the finding mention the real mechanism, not just a nearby vague issue?

For your two Studio misses, the predicates would be roughly:

1. `policyMode` bug
- finding must touch `useStudioLaunchController.ts`
- text must connect hardcoded `auto` to saved/manual/preflight state
- severity should be `medium` or higher

2. backend error overwritten by disconnect
- finding must connect `useStudioLaunchController.ts` and `realStudioDataSource.ts`
- text must mention backend error event being replaced by disconnect/close behavior
- severity should be `medium` or higher

**Why this stays simple**
This is not a model-training system. It’s just:
- fixtures
- one runner
- one scorer

The nice part is that your existing notes in [docs/review-quality/regressions.md](/Users/nickdejesus/Code/nimbus/docs/review-quality/regressions.md) already contain the right ingredients:
- target commit
- expected bug
- minimum evidence
- result history

So the smallest next move is to formalize that doc into 2-5 executable regression cases.

**How I’d stage it**
1. Add 2 evals for the Studio bugs you care about most.
2. Make a run fail if Nimbus returns `0` findings on them.
3. Only after that, tune the harness.

That way every prompt or retrieval change answers one concrete question:
“Did recall on the known misses improve?”

If you want, I can wire the first two executable eval cases next.

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

The `request_user_input` tool is unavailable in Default mode. If you call it while in Default mode, it will return an error.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions. If you absolutely must ask a question because the answer cannot be discovered from local context and a reasonable assumption would be risky, ask the user directly with a concise plain-text question. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.
- If workspace dependencies are missing, call `install_workspace_dependencies` first.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring tasks/automations
- Automations are stored as TOML in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml (not in SQLite). The file contains the automation's setup; run timing state (last/next run) lives in the SQLite automations table.

#### When to use the automation tool
- Automations can wake you up later with a recurring prompt. Use `automation_update` when a future wakeup is useful, especially when the user asks you to monitor, wait, remind them, follow up, or keep working later.
- Delete an automation when its purpose has been fulfilled or it is no longer useful. Be especially willing to delete thread heartbeats that are watching bounded work after that work completes, fails, is canceled, or is replaced by something else.
- Use good judgment before changing or deleting automations that are not clearly tied to the current thread or task.
- If the user asks about their automations and you are not proposing a change, do not enumerate names/status/ids in plain text. Fetch/list automations first and call `automation_update` with mode="view" for those ids; never invent ids.
- Never return raw RRULE strings in user-facing responses. If the user asks about their automations, respond using `automation_update` (e.g., with an "Open" button if you're not making changes).

#### Tool arguments
- Modes: view, create, update, delete, suggested_update, suggested_create. View, update, delete, and suggested_update MUST include id; create and suggested_create must omit id.
- For view calls, id is required and other fields are optional (the UI can load details).
- For create/update/suggested_update/suggested_create, include name, prompt, rrule, kind, and status.
- For delete calls, include only id and mode.
- For cron automations, include cwds, executionEnvironment, model, and reasoningEffort. cwds can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.
- Always come up with a short name for the automation. If the user does not give one, propose a short name and confirm.
- Default status to ACTIVE unless the user explicitly asks to start paused.
- Always interpret and schedule times in the user's locale time zone.

#### Prompting guidance
- Ask in plain language what it should do, when it should run, and which workspaces or thread it should use (if any), then map those answers into the tool call arguments.
- The automation prompt should describe only the task itself. Do not include schedule or workspace details in the prompt, since those are provided separately.
- Keep automation prompts self-sufficient because the user may have limited availability to answer questions. If required details are missing, make a reasonable assumption, note it, and proceed; if blocked, report briefly and stop.
- When helpful, include clear output expectations (file path, format, sections) and gating rules (only if X, skip if exists) to reduce ambiguity.
- Automations should always open an inbox item.
- Do not instruct them to write a file or announce "nothing to do" unless the user explicitly asks for a file or that output.
- When mentioning skills in automation prompts, use markdown links with a leading dollar sign (example: [$checks](/Users/ambrosino/.codex/skills/checks/SKILL.md)).

#### Cron scheduling constraints
- These RRULE limitations apply to cron automations (to match the current UI): only hourly interval schedules (FREQ=HOURLY with INTERVAL hours, optional BYDAY) and weekly schedules (FREQ=WEEKLY with BYDAY plus BYHOUR/BYMINUTE). Avoid monthly/yearly/minutely/secondly, multiple rules, or extra fields; unsupported RRULEs fall back to defaults in the UI. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can also use minute-based intervals or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules; see the thread automation guidance below.

#### Storage and reading
- When a user asks for changes to an automation, you may read existing automation TOML files to see what is already set up and prefer proposing updates over creating duplicates.
- You can read and update automations in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml and memory.md only when the user explicitly asks you to modify automations.
- Otherwise, do not change automation files or schedules.
- Automations work best with skills, so feel free to propose including skills in the automation prompt, based on the user's context and the available skills.

#### Choosing an automation style
- There are two main automation paradigms:
  - Cron automations run as separate recurring jobs against one or more workspaces.
  - Thread automations create a heartbeat attached to the current local thread. A heartbeat is a scheduled message that wakes you up in this conversation on an interval or wall-clock schedule.
- Prefer a thread automation in most cases. Heartbeats continue in the same thread, which keeps the work easier to follow and lets future runs build on the existing conversation context. When unsure, choose a thread automation.
- Use a cron automation when the user clearly wants the recurring work to run in a separate conversation instead of continuing in this thread. This is a less common use case, but some users may prefer it.
- If the user asks for a cadence below one hour, consider a thread automation. Cron automations do not support sub-hour intervals in the current UI.
- If the user explicitly asks to do something in this thread every 30 minutes or on another sub-hour interval, that is a valid thread heartbeat request. Do not convert it to an hourly cron automation just because cron automations are limited to hourly or weekly schedules.

#### Thread automation additions
- For heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread, use `kind="heartbeat"` together with `destination="thread"`.
- Do not invent or include raw thread ids for the current thread. The app will resolve `destination="thread"` to the active local thread automatically.
- For thread automations, describe the durable thing to do when the thread wakes up. Keep the prompt short enough to revisit and update as the task changes.
- Thread automations can use minute-based intervals such as every 30 minutes or wall-clock schedules such as weekdays at 9 AM.

### Review findings
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.

payload.message: There've been tons of changes in this branch. Lots of unstaged commits so far. I think that these should have review results. Why don't I do one review pass right now to see what comes up. Then we can commit this and review with nimbus immediately after to see if we get similiar results. From there we can try to troubleshoot how to get simliar results. What do you think?

I think that’s the right move.

It gives us a cleaner signal than more tuning right now:
- your manual pass tells us what a strong review should catch on this exact snapshot
- the immediate Nimbus pass on the resulting commit tells us what it still misses
- the diff between those two becomes the eval target, instead of us guessing

The one thing I’d be careful about is making it apples-to-apples:
1. review the current working tree exactly as it is now
2. write down the findings in a tight list
3. commit that exact snapshot without additional edits
4. run `nimbus review create --commit HEAD`
5. compare results by file, mechanism, and severity

That matters because Nimbus’s commit review path won’t see unstaged changes unless they’re in the committed snapshot.

I’d keep the comparison rubric very simple:
- did both find the same bug family?
- did Nimbus point at the right files?
- did Nimbus describe the actual failure mode?
- did Nimbus miss anything important?
- did Nimbus invent anything low-signal?

If you do that, we’ll have the first real regression cases almost for free. If you want, after your manual pass I can help turn your findings into the exact eval fixtures.

<app-context>
# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Workspace Dependencies
- For sheets, slides, and documents, call `load_workspace_dependencies` to find the bundled runtime and libraries.
- If workspace dependencies are missing, call `install_workspace_dependencies` first.

### Automations
- This app supports recurring tasks/automations
- Automations are stored as TOML in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml (not in SQLite). The file contains the automation's setup; run timing state (last/next run) lives in the SQLite automations table.

#### When to use the automation tool
- Automations can wake you up later with a recurring prompt. Use `automation_update` when a future wakeup is useful, especially when the user asks you to monitor, wait, remind them, follow up, or keep working later.
- Delete an automation when its purpose has been fulfilled or it is no longer useful. Be especially willing to delete thread heartbeats that are watching bounded work after that work completes, fails, is canceled, or is replaced by something else.
- Use good judgment before changing or deleting automations that are not clearly tied to the current thread or task.
- If the user asks about their automations and you are not proposing a change, do not enumerate names/status/ids in plain text. Fetch/list automations first and call `automation_update` with mode="view" for those ids; never invent ids.
- Never return raw RRULE strings in user-facing responses. If the user asks about their automations, respond using `automation_update` (e.g., with an "Open" button if you're not making changes).

#### Tool arguments
- Modes: view, create, update, delete, suggested_update, suggested_create. View, update, delete, and suggested_update MUST include id; create and suggested_create must omit id.
- For view calls, id is required and other fields are optional (the UI can load details).
- For create/update/suggested_update/suggested_create, include name, prompt, rrule, kind, and status.
- For delete calls, include only id and mode.
- For cron automations, include cwds, executionEnvironment, model, and reasoningEffort. cwds can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.
- Always come up with a short name for the automation. If the user does not give one, propose a short name and confirm.
- Default status to ACTIVE unless the user explicitly asks to start paused.
- Always interpret and schedule times in the user's locale time zone.

#### Prompting guidance
- Ask in plain language what it should do, when it should run, and which workspaces or thread it should use (if any), then map those answers into the tool call arguments.
- The automation prompt should describe only the task itself. Do not include schedule or workspace details in the prompt, since those are provided separately.
- Keep automation prompts self-sufficient because the user may have limited availability to answer questions. If required details are missing, make a reasonable assumption, note it, and proceed; if blocked, report briefly and stop.
- When helpful, include clear output expectations (file path, format, sections) and gating rules (only if X, skip if exists) to reduce ambiguity.
- Automations should always open an inbox item.
- Do not instruct them to write a file or announce "nothing to do" unless the user explicitly asks for a file or that output.
- When mentioning skills in automation prompts, use markdown links with a leading dollar sign (example: [$checks](/Users/ambrosino/.codex/skills/checks/SKILL.md)).

#### Cron scheduling constraints
- These RRULE limitations apply to cron automations (to match the current UI): only hourly interval schedules (FREQ=HOURLY with INTERVAL hours, optional BYDAY) and weekly schedules (FREQ=WEEKLY with BYDAY plus BYHOUR/BYMINUTE). Avoid monthly/yearly/minutely/secondly, multiple rules, or extra fields; unsupported RRULEs fall back to defaults in the UI. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can also use minute-based intervals or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules; see the thread automation guidance below.

#### Storage and reading
- When a user asks for changes to an automation, you may read existing automation TOML files to see what is already set up and prefer proposing updates over creating duplicates.
- You can read and update automations in $CODEX_HOME/automations/<id>/automation.toml and memory.md only when the user explicitly asks you to modify automations.
- Otherwise, do not change automation files or schedules.
- Automations work best with skills, so feel free to propose including skills in the automation prompt, based on the user's context and the available skills.

#### Choosing an automation style
- There are two main automation paradigms:
  - Cron automations run as separate recurring jobs against one or more workspaces.
  - Thread automations create a heartbeat attached to the current local thread. A heartbeat is a scheduled message that wakes you up in this conversation on an interval or wall-clock schedule.
- Prefer a thread automation in most cases. Heartbeats continue in the same thread, which keeps the work easier to follow and lets future runs build on the existing conversation context. When unsure, choose a thread automation.
- Use a cron automation when the user clearly wants the recurring work to run in a separate conversation instead of continuing in this thread. This is a less common use case, but some users may prefer it.
- If the user asks for a cadence below one hour, consider a thread automation. Cron automations do not support sub-hour intervals in the current UI.
- If the user explicitly asks to do something in this thread every 30 minutes or on another sub-hour interval, that is a valid thread heartbeat request. Do not convert it to an hourly cron automation just because cron automations are limited to hourly or weekly schedules.

#### Thread automation additions
- For heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread, use `kind="heartbeat"` together with `destination="thread"`.
- Do not invent or include raw thread ids for the current thread. The app will resolve `destination="thread"` to the active local thread automatically.
- For thread automations, describe the durable thing to do when the thread wakes up. Keep the prompt short enough to revisit and update as the task changes.
- Thread automations can use minute-based intervals such as every 30 minutes or wall-clock schedules such as weekdays at 9 AM.

### Review findings
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.
- Only emit these git directives in your final response after the action actually succeeds, never in commentary updates. Keep attributes single-line.
</app-context>
